Voss heard it, and heard what the Chantry would have silenced, and let the sound settle into the place in his chest that had once held the joy of the lever.

It did not empty out. It held both. That, too, was a kind of truth.

He went down into the quarter, and he did not let his hand shake.

chapters.name: Rewiring the Design
chapters.content:
The candle had burned to a nub, and Voss had not noticed. Above the chandler's shop he worked by its last light, the cracked compass under his elbow, Gref's parchment spread before him. On one face: the Chantry's design—forty-seven points, the accelerant lines laid high against the flood, a quarter given to fire. It was done. Three days until the new moon. The Chantry would see it and call it surgery.

He turned the sheet.

The Chantry believed he was still refining their fire-lines. He was. Every point on the front face was exact, faithful, ready to be praised. But a line on paper was only a line until the fire chose which way to run, and Voss had spent fifteen years learning how to make fire choose.

On the reverse, in the cramped ant-foot hand Pella had mocked, the mirror of the design. The Salt Stair's line—the throat of the quarter, where flame would close like a hand—did not end in the Hanging Market. It ran down through the black water beneath the Flats, along old channels the surveyors had never charted, and came up under the dry-docks where the Chantry's whale-grease warehouses stood on tarred pilings above the harbor; it rose again in the foundations of the Spire of Charters, in the deep timber cribs the ledgers never mentioned.

It was delicate, mathematical work. The accelerant lines had to be laid high enough that the twice-daily tide would not wash them out, low enough that no one walking the Flats would see the new channels. Each junction had to be faithful to the Chantry's plan—right up to the moment the flow passed the hidden switch and did not reach the quarter at all. He measured twice with Gref's twine, checked his figures against the tide tables, drew and redrew the switches until the flip was as clean and inevitable as a compass needle finding north.

The pleasure rose in his chest like a coal fanned red: the godlike thrill, a world made and unmade at the turn of his wrist. He let himself feel it. For fifteen years it had meant Gullrot—the forty-seven points blooming at once, the crier's voice cut short, the joy he had never confessed. Now it meant something else. The same fire, the same hand, the same beautiful design—but bound to a different purpose. He was not burning the Flats. He was burning the men who had drawn the line around the Flats and called it surgery.

The memory came up through the floor of his chest, as it always did when the work was finest. After Gullrot he had walked through the ash, not from horror but because the cartographer in him needed to see what his lines had made. He had walked through the silence and found the baker's stall. The fire had passed it at the line's edge—a hair's breadth he could have shifted, had chosen not to, because the line would not have been beautiful. The oven was still warm. Inside sat a loaf, untouched, perfect, as if the baker had set it to rise and meant to come back. Voss had stood in the warm smell of bread and had not eaten the loaf. He had left it to go cold, and told no one.

He understood what the memory was: a promise broken before it was made. The baker had fed him as a child, and Voss had let his stall stand on the line because the geometry was cleaner that way, and he had called it justice. He could not undo that. The loaf would be cold in his mind as long as he lived. But he could refuse to repeat it—could make certain this fire left no warm oven and no untouched loaf behind it. The vow did not feel like redemption. It felt like a hand closing on the lever for a different reason.

He blew out the candle.

Dawn found him at the water's edge, where Pella had told him to look. "You want to see the Flats, you should see them from the water. That's where they're honest." He took a dory from the chandler's slip and rowed out past the leaning tenements until he found what the maps never showed: a tunnel mouth in the seawall, cut with a mason's patience, hidden by a fishing net hung to dry. Iskra Venn came out of it as he drifted past, a knife in her fist and then not. She looked at him with the flat measuring gaze of a woman who had never been fooled by a disguise, only by the man wearing it.

"Count-man," she said. "You row like a surveyor."

"I've been told I read like one too."

"Asking about my tunnels again? Last time I said I mend nets for the chapel."

"I know your nets," Voss said. "I need your tunnels."

The knife came back into her hand.

"Not for the Flats," he said quickly, and the word *not* hung in the air between them longer than the others. He took the field-book page from his coat—the page the surveyors had abandoned in Gref's cellar—and handed it to her across the water. She read it with her lips moving, once, twice. When she looked up, her eyes were not measuring him. They were asking what kind of man carried a document like that in his coat.

"The ground is iron," Voss said. "The fire is meant to be the shovel. I was contracted to draw the lines that would clear it." He let the half-truth stand; it was the truest thing he could say without saying the whole. "I've decided the lines will go elsewhere. The Chantry's dry-docks. The pilings under the Spire. But I can't lay the new channels without going under the quarter, and you're the only one who knows where the water runs."

Iskra was silent a long moment. The tide turned around the dory's hull, and Voss felt the water shift beneath him, the whole map of the Flats tilting on its axis.

"You're asking me to trust you with the weight of it," she said. Not a question.

"Yes."

"You, who came down the Salt Stair in a dead warden's coat to count us like fuel loads. You, who carried the plan for our death in your pocket while you ate bread in our chapel." She said it without heat, listing the contents of a cargo hold. "What do I tell my people?"

Voss looked at the tunnel mouth, black against the seawall. Behind it ran the passages that would carry the Flats' children and wounded out of the way when the chaos came. What he needed from her was not forgiveness, not belief—it was the direction of the design.

"Tell them a tide of upheaval is coming," he said. "Tell them to be ready to move through your tunnels when the signal comes. Not before, not after. Trust the timing, because I'll be the one who lights it and aims it."

"Who are you?" she asked. Not a demand. The first time she had asked as a person, not a smuggler weighing a threat.

Voss pulled the sheet from his coat and unfolded it, letting her see the reverse—the forty-seven lines of the Chantry's plan and the redrawn channels that carried them away from the Flats, out under the harbor, into the foundations of the city. Not the whole truth; that was not hers to carry. But the flip of it, the beautiful terrible re-aiming of the lever: that he gave her.

"I'm the man who drew the first one," he said. "I'll be damned if I draw this one the same way."

Iskra looked at the paper a long moment. Then she nodded once, sharply, the way a captain gives an order to the tide. "The tunnels run from the Salt Stair to the chapel and down under the harbor. If you want your lines laid where the surveyors won't look, you'll have to come down into the dark with me and see for yourself."

Voss stepped from the dory to the seawall, and the net moved under his hand like the skin of something alive. "Show me."

The dark swallowed them both, and Voss went down into it with the map of the flip folded inside his coat, the vow loud in his chest: no untouched loaf. Not this time. He would see to it himself.

chapters.name: The Congregation of the Deep
chapters.content:
The meeting took place in the drowned chapel at low tide, the nave ankle-deep in the water that would not leave the quarter's bones. Voss stood before the altar with Iskra at his shoulder, unrolling a stained chart of the district—evacuation routes, not fire-lines, though the two had begun to look alike to him.

Preacher Odrin studied the marks without touching the paper. His hands were a fisherman's, scarred at the knuckles. "Three ways out. You expect half the Flats to crawl through a bricked-up drain because a count-man says a tide is coming?"

"Yes."

"What tide?"

Voss met his eyes. "The kind the city has always been good at."

Brother Sathen stood apart, the birthmark under his left eye black in the candle-light. He had known Voss's face from the arsonist gallery under glass, had named him burn-man without unkindness, and the name sat in the room now like a stone in the shallows. Sathen said nothing. He did not need to. His silence was the price of the plan.

So Voss gave them what he could. The Salt Stair tunnels meeting the chapel crypt. The Hanging Market cellars feeding Iskra's black-water channel. The flensing-sheds behind the bone-yard opening onto the seaward breakwater. He drew safe houses with the pencil stub worn to a nub, marking each with a circle no different from the one he had once drawn around a fire's reach. Patterns. He had always trusted patterns. Now he was trusting them with the weight of a quarter he had been paid to burn.

"When the signal comes," Iskra said, "you move. You do not stop for your nets or your boots or your grandfather's cup. You take the children and you go. The tunnels will hold."

Odrin looked from Iskra to Voss, and the lines of his face settled. "The chapel will be ready."

Voss blew out the candle and let the dark take them.

---

Dawn found him on the mud-flats with a fish-net in his hands and Pella Three-Holes watching him from a barrel, bare feet swinging.

"You're doing it wrong," she said. "You started at the wrong hole."

"All holes are holes."

"No, they got a order." She slid off the barrel, took the net from him without asking, and held the tear up to the light, threading the twine with the certainty of a child who had mended more nets than she had owned. Voss let himself be taught. His fingers, which could lay an accelerant line within a hair's breadth of a foundation, learned the crossing knot she showed him in ten heartbeats' work, and the net began to close like skin over a wound.

"Mending," Pella said approvingly. "You're not so useless, count-man."

And the memory came up from the water beneath them, unbidden: a seven-year-old girl at the quarantine line, the doll in her hands flaking like ash, turning to walk back into Gullrot because no one would let her through. Voss had watched from the tower. He had not called down. He had not gone to the gate. The schedule had been precise.

He tied off the knot and ran his thumb along the mend—smooth, unbroken. Not the same. Not the same at all.

Pella was watching him with a child's frank attention. "You got a sad face, count-man."

"Heard one says so."

She shrugged, took the net, and slung it over her shoulder. "You can mend my net again sometime. If you want."

She was gone before he could answer, and the sound of her bare feet on the wet boards followed him all the way to the drowned chapel.

---

The sermon began at the turn of the tide, when the water in the nave had just begun to fall. Voss had not intended to stay. But Sathen touched his sleeve, and Odrin raised his hands, and the room fell silent as the flood-line.

There were no candles. There could be none; light above the water-line was a signal to the Chantry's eyes. The congregation of the deep stood ankle-deep in the ringing dark, and Mael Odrin preached the mercy of the deep—a thing that takes and gives back, that does not ask what you have done before it swallows you, that holds the drowned and the lost and the escaped whole in its one wide breath. He prayed for the sick by their fevers, for the hidden whalers by the seal of Iskra's tunnels, for the children by the names they had. He prayed for the count-man whose census had not once asked an offering.

Beside Voss, a woman prayed for the city above them. A city, she said, that wore fine words like a coat and underneath was naked. Voss closed his eyes.

The crier's voice came back to him as clearly as if the boy stood in the chapel nave, reading from the edict Voss had helped to write: *For the health of Veyra, and the excision of the fever's root, the quarter of Gullrot is hereby cleansed. Those who remain within the lines are deemed to have consented.*

He had written "consented." He had written "cleansed." The words were clean, surgical, bright as a drawn line. And he had let the crier finish before he pulled the lever, because the boy's voice was the final chord of the design, and the design was beautiful.

The Chantry's clerk had spoken in the same tongue: "surgery," "pestilence," "rats with knives." The quarter's pestilence is convenient. The claims are not. He recognized the rhetoric because he had authored it, young and proud and sure of his hands.

Odrin's voice went on in the dark, calling down mercy on the drowned, and Voss stood among the congregation of the deep and felt the edict language peel off him like ash off a beam. He had written those words. He would not write them again.

---

After the sermon, a fishmonger whose stall stood at the edge of the Hanging Market took Voss by the arm and drew him to a plank table in the lee of a tenement. There was salt bread, and a bowl of oil, and a pot of small black fish that tasted of smoke. A family—mother, father, two children, a grandfather with one eye and no boots—pressed bread into his hands as if he were a guest, not the architect of their last dawn. Voss ate with them, and the bread was warm, and inside his coat lay the field-book page that would send fire to the Spire instead of their roofs.

He did not deserve their thanks. That was not the point. The point was that they were alive, and warm, and unafraid in his presence, and he was going to keep them that way. No untouched loaf. Not this time. When the fire came, it would find the men who had drawn the circle around these families and called it surgery.

He set down the bread and looked around the table—the grandfather's good eye, the children's salt-crusted hair, Pella's absent laugh somewhere beyond the lamplight—and he let himself measure it. For the first time since Gullrot he was counting people and not fuel loads.

The congregation of the deep had prayed for him. They would never know what they had prayed for. But Voss did, and he carried it out of the lamplight with him into the dark, down to the water's edge, where Iskra waited with the tunnel-mouth's net in her hand and the tide turning beneath them.

"It's done," she said. "The plan is laid."

"Not yet," Voss said. "But it will be."

He had two days until the new moon. Two days to be sure the design was true. He went down into the dark with her, into the water-sound and the bricked-up silence, and the last thing he heard before the tunnel closed over his head was a child's high hollow voice, counting toward forty-seven, somewhere in the quarter he had chosen to save.

chapters.name: The Spring Tithe
chapters.content:
The night of the Spring Leviathan tithe smelled of whale-oil and festival smoke, and all of Veyra had climbed to the roofs to watch it burn.

They brought Voss through the crowd like a relic. The thin clerk walked ahead with the fire-map rolled under his arm, and two wharfmen walked behind with hands ready at their belts. Torchlight slid across the shoulders of the crowd, the lanterns strung from every eave, the oil-banners snapping in the harbor wind. A child pointed at him. The whole city was dressed for a spectacle, and Voss knew what spectacle they thought they had paid for.

The Spire of Charters rose above the quay, its windows blazing. Inside, the tribunal waited in the aerie—the magistrate with his ledger-ink fingers, the magnate with rings sunk into his flesh, the clerk who said nothing. They did not speak to him now. They only nodded at the staircase, and the wharfmen walked him up.

The Ember Gallery was high and round, a room built for exactly one purpose. In its center stood the ignition mechanism: an iron wheel, a counterweight, a single lever rising from a brass collar. Lanterns no bigger than fists burned on the walls. Beyond the west window, the Drowned Flats lay black and quiet under the new moon, the scattered lamps of fish-sellers and the drowned chapel's single rushlight pricking the dark. To the north, the harbor glittered with the tithe fleet's lights. To the south, the dry-docks crouched in shadow, the Chantry's warehouses fat with whale-grease and tarred pilings.

Voss's hand found the lever. It was warm. The same kind of lever he had pulled fifteen years ago. The same counterweight, greased. The same design.

The thrill arrived like a spark to oil.

It ran up his arm and into his chest, whispering in the voice that had always known how to speak: one fire, your name cut in stone, the city rebuilt in the shape of your lines. He could feel the plan laid out beneath his feet like a second map of Veyra—forty-seven points, the alleys he had charted, the chandler's shop, the bone-yard, the Salt Stair. His hand tightened. The magistrate had called it surgery. The magnate had promised a monument. The clerk would write the record, and the record would say Voss had saved the city twice.

He looked down at the Flats, and memory came up out of the dark.

The girl with the broken doll stood at the Carmine Gate, turned away, her doll's paint flaking like ash. She had looked up at his window. He had not called down. He had not gone to the gate.

The baker's loaf stood warm in the oven at the edge of the fire-line, untouched because Voss had said I don't take gifts. He could have shifted the line a hair's breadth. He had not, because the line would not have been beautiful.

The crier's voice rang against the stones: For the health of Veyra, and the excision of the fever's root, the quarter of Gullrot is hereby cleansed. Those who remain within the lines are deemed to have consented. Voss had written those words. He had let the boy finish, and the boy had nodded up at the tower as if saying, I have done my part. Do yours.

Then Pella's face, laughing, salt-bright. Pella teaching him the crossing knot on the mud-flats. Pella saying, You got a sad face, count-man. Pella asking if she was a tally or a name. Pella's bare feet running from him into the quarter he had been paid to burn.

The field-book page was still in his coat. Tidal iron. The claims are not. The Chantry's ledger had more than one face, and so did the map in the clerk's hand—the faithful face, the obedient fire-line, the design that would end at the Hanging Market with its dead-end courts and its children. But the reverse of that sheet lay in the dark beneath the city, laid by Iskra's hands in the tunnels, waiting for him.

The thrill was still there. It had never once left him. He could feel it licking under his ribs, the old godlike joy of the lever, the perfect geometry of a controlled inferno. He knew he would never be rid of it. He had named it, and naming it had not killed it.

But the hand had always had a choice.

"Pull it, architect," the magnate called from the gallery above, his voice thick with oil and patience. "The city is watching."

Voss looked at the Flats once more. A single lamp had moved in the dark quarter—a signal lantern, low and quick, answering the plan he had given them. The chapel would be empty of candles. The fishmonger would be shepherding the one-eyed grandfather toward the flensing-sheds. Pella would be at Iskra's hip, counting steps under the tide.

He thought of the untouched loaf, the warm oven, the promise kept this time or broken forever.

Then his hand moved.

He did not pull toward the Hanging Market. He pulled the lever down through its full travel, and beneath the brass collar he felt the second catch, the one he had cut himself, the hidden switch no one had thought to look for because no one had ever believed the burn-man would turn.

The counterweight dropped. The wheel spun. Somewhere below the city, oil began to run.

The first sound was small—a hiss, a suck of air, a chain of clicks racing along the hidden channels beneath the harbor. Voss watched the Flats, waiting for the bloom that would not come. The black quarter stayed black. The single rushlight in the drowned chapel went out, one by one the fish-sellers' lamps vanished, and the Drowned Flats emptied themselves into the earth like water through a sieve.

A voice above him said, "Where is the fire?"

Voss did not answer. He was watching the dry-docks.

They went up together, as he had drawn them—the tarred pilings, the whale-grease warehouses, the storehouses stuffed with sailcloth and blubber and the Chantry's careful ledgers. The flame ran along his lines the way it had always run, beautiful and exact, and it found the deep timber cribs beneath the Spire of Charters, and it bit.

The floor shivered.

The magnate said, "What have you done?"

Voss turned from the window. The thrill was still singing in his chest, hotter than it had ever been—the joy, the power, the perfect control—but aimed at last. He had not become innocent. He had become a different kind of incendiary. The fire would not touch the quarter he had charted as people. It would touch the men who had drawn the circle and called it surgery.

Smoke threaded up between the floorboards. Far below, the foundations of the Spire of Charters groaned like a whale turning in its sleep.

The clerk stood at the door with his hand on the handle, his face the color of tallow.

Voss walked past him, out of the Ember Gallery, down the shaking stair into the gathering dark, with the sound of the Spring Tithe breaking into screams behind him, and the black dawn of the Drowned Flats opening ahead.

chapters.name: The Flipped Design
chapters.content:
He went down through the shaking dark as the Spire began to die around him. Smoke came down the stair ahead of him, a tide finding its level before the water does, and underneath the smoke ran the building's complaint: stone grinding on stone, iron letting go in long, drawn howls. Voss moved with one hand on the wall. He did not hurry. Hurry was a confession of doubt, and the design left nothing to doubt.

He knew the fire's progress by the sound it made, the way another man knows an hour by the angle of the light. A window burst three flights up, glass ringing off the stairwell. A beam found a corridor and came out singing. Beneath it all, in the drowned place where the sea lay against the foundation cribs, the fire was eating timber and the building was settling down into its appetite like a beast sinking into a bog. The stone had a heartbeat under his boots. He had put it there. He had drawn the line of it from the Salt Stair down through the black water of Iskra's channels, up under the dry-docks where the whale-grease warehouses sat on tarred pilings, and into the deep cribs. Iskra's hands had laid his ink in the dark while the Chantry's surveyors looked at the wrong lines, and the thought of that—her patience, her trust in paper—did something to his chest that he refused to name.

At the third landing a window stood open to the night. Voss stopped without deciding to. The body knows a reckoning before the mind will admit to one.

The harbor was on fire.

Not the water. The water was a black mirror, and the fire used it as a second canvas, casting the whole design doubled and rocked by the current: the dry-docks open to the sky like a rib-cage, the whale-grease storehouses burned white at the heart, flame running from them along the tarred gangways exactly where he had traced it, an ink-line taking light in the order he had written it out, in a hand he had kept sharp through fifteen years of waiting. This is what a map becomes when it is believed, he thought. A living thing. A thing that goes on moving after the hands that drew it are gone.

The thrill was in him, hot and alive. It had not diminished in fifteen years. He stood at the window with the harbor burning before him and felt the pleasure rise in his chest—the old engine of his ruin, the thing that made him pull the lever at Gullrot and would always have made him pull it again. He did not look away from it. He had spent fifteen years declining to name it. Now he named it: it was joy, and it was his, and he had aimed it. The joy did not make him innocent. Nothing would. But it had finally drawn a true line.

He touched the field-book page inside his coat. Tidal iron. *The quarter's pestilence is convenient. The claims are not.* They had looked at the Flats and seen an obstruction to be removed, and they had written it in good ink in a good hand, and it had almost been enough. He had answered with better ink and a worse hand. The symmetry was not justice. He did not pretend it was. It was arithmetic. But arithmetic had saved the children.

Fifteen years ago he had walked the ash of Gullrot at dawn and come to the baker's stall at the edge of the fire-line. The oven had still been warm. The loaf inside had been untouched, flour dusted along its scored top, and he had stood over it for a long time unable to take it. He had told himself he had not earned it. The truth was worse: he had drawn the fire-line for its beauty, and the stall had stood on it, and he had let it burn rather than spoil the line by a hair's breadth. He had refused the loaf before the fire and refused it again after, because taking it would have meant the baker was a man, and the beautiful line was only ash.

From the stairwell above and behind him, the magnate's voice came down thin with distance, a scream wearing a coat: "The oil—all the oil! The warehouses—we are ruined—"

Below, the city saw it too. The rooftops of Veyra were packed with the Spring Tithe crowds who had come to see a quarter burned and were instead watching the Chantry's own flame climb the Spire of Charters. He heard it in the thin human alarm drifting up through the roar, the way a string of horses shies at a smell it cannot place. They would understand soon enough. They would decide who to hunt.

Voss did not turn. The aerie's great window was above him and to his left, an arched eye of burning glass, and the fire had climbed high enough to light the figures at the rail. He could read them only as shapes. The magnate, hands upraised like a man begging tribute from a god he had never believed in. The magistrate, standing perfectly still, which was somehow worse than any screaming. And the clerk—the thin, unblinking clerk—holding the scroll. The faithful map. The beautiful plan. Voss's hand had drawn that sheet in two directions, and the clerk was holding only the direction he had believed in.

The magistrate's voice, surfacing through the roar: "He gave us the plan. He gave us the plan, and then he—"

The clerk's fingers moved. Even at that distance Voss could imagine the exact motion: the small wrist-turn, the vellum folding back, the light falling on the reverse of the sheet—the hidden line descending from the Salt Stair, the black-water channel, the dry-dock run, the crib. The line that made sense of all the rest. The clerk would find his own death in that geometry. Voss had seen the man's unblinking eyes in three interviews; he knew how they would move across the ink, left to right, like a man reading a prayer. Then they would go back to the beginning, and all at once he would see the signature.

He never saw whether the clerk read it. A section of roof came down somewhere between them, and the noise of it swallowed the glass out of the window frame; Voss felt it through the stones, through his ribs, a bass note struck on the whole body of the Spire. The building was done considering. It had heard the verdict from its foundations.

He turned from the window—and stopped, because the window faced the harbor, and beyond the channel lay the Flats, and he needed to see it once before the dark closed over him.

The quarter was dark. A black band against the red sky. Then it was not. Lamps went up along the breakwater in a string, small gold points moving into the open air: the congregation of the deep emerging from Odrin's tunnels behind the bone-yard, carrying their lights up into the night. Pella would be among them. The plan had said children first, tunnels that would hold, and the plan was true. He watched the lamps with the Chantry's burning towering behind them, and both were his design. The fire: drawn to fall on power. The lamps: drawn to rise at the water's edge. The line between them ran through his sternum, and he stood on both sides of it, and that was the whole verdict. He was not a hero. He had not earned the word. He was a just arsonist, and the distinction might exist only in the direction of the flame, but he had aimed it at last.

The thrill was still there. He had stopped expecting it to leave. A man can cut down a rotten belief and still feel the axe sing; the sin is not in the singing, but in choosing what to fell.

He went down.

The stair turned, and turned again, and the smoke grew thicker, until he dropped below the line of it and the night came clean and salt. The service stairs were older than the rest of the Spire, the stone worn to a gutter by two hundred years of feet, and the fire had not reached them yet, though its voice followed him down like a hound at heel. On the next landing he passed the Chartroom door. It stood open. The Chantry's municipal maps lay in their racks, the whole false geography of their claim—the quarter as a stain, the claims as holy writ—and the fire had found them. The edges of the map tables kindled, curled, went black. Voss stood in the doorway for one breath and watched the lies burn like any other paper, and thought: *that is all they ever were.*

Then he left the staircase and took the water-vaults. He knew the way without a light: the smell of bilge, the slap of the harbor against the sea-wall, the distance counted in his ankles as the water rose. He had mapped this route from the wrong side, freed by the Chantry into purpose, and Iskra had hauled him through it once to show him the turn he would need. The tunnel mouth opened in the sea-wall like a wound, black water licking at its stone lip. Cold came up at him from it, dense with salt and rot and, underneath all that, the smell of lamp-oil—his handiwork, already moving. The tide was at the turn. He had mapped the high-water hours into the plan; the channel would flood within the bell, and the fire was buying him the time to be ahead of it.

He put one hand on the wet stone. In his coat, Pella's string of sprats crackled faintly against the canvas, a small dry music. He had eaten the warm loaf at the fishmonger's table; he could feel that kindness sitting in him where the fire could not reach. No untouched loaf, he thought. Not this time. Not ever.

Behind him the Spire of Charters made a sound full of stone. It was not a groan and not a scream. It was the sound of enormous weights beginning the long arithmetic of falling, and the water in the vaults heard it too, and shivered. Voss did not look back. The sliding dark of the tunnel took the shape of a man and held it—a hand on the wall, a compass broken in his pocket, a map of people drawn on the inside of him—and then the water rose around his knees, and the dark closed over his head, and he went on.

chapters.name: Through the Tunnels
chapters.content:
The water closed over his head and the dark was absolute.

The channel ran beneath the sea-wall, older than the Spire, older than the Chantry's grip. Voss knew it from the surveyors' pages, from the pilings charted in the Chartroom, from the way the tide breathed through it like a lung. He had laid his fire-lines along this black water, and now the black water carried him.

The tide was at the turn, pushing behind him, a patient hand in the small of his back. He did not swim so much as let the flood carry him, one hand trailing the wall, counting joists by touch. The channel narrowed; the roof dropped; the water rose to his chin, to his lips, and he tilted his head back and kept moving, because stopping was not in the design. Behind him, through stone and water, the Spire groaned—not a noise but a shudder. Voss kept counting.

The tunnel forked. Left: the old culvert that fed the bone-yard breakwater. Right: black water, deeper, under the dry-docks he had already burned. He took the left, finding the iron rungs the surveyors had marked collapsed but were not; he had climbed them three nights ago, hanging a line of his own.

His head broke water into a low brick vault, ankle-deep in salt-scummed tide. Light came from nowhere and everywhere—a crack overhead where the Spire's burning foundations bled orange. Voss stood in the shallow water and listened.

Feet. Many of them, moving.

He pressed into the shadow of the pilings, hand on the tin badge at his throat—the shore-warden's badge that meant nothing now. If the Chantry's enforcers had found the tunnels before the people—

But the feet were unshod, and a child's voice was counting.

"…thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty—"

Quell. The boy who played Burn-Man, counting toward the number Voss had made famous.

Voss stepped out of the shadow. "Quell."

The counting stopped; the tunnel went still. Then a familiar voice: "Burn-man."

Iskra Venn came up the vault at the head of a line of refugees—mud to the knees, whaler's knife loose in her fist, face lit from above by the orange bleed. Behind her the tunnel muttered with footfalls and held breath.

"You're alive," Iskra said: not a greeting, but an accusation she had not decided to drop.

"The design holds," Voss said. "The Flats?"

"Empty," she said. "You'd know, if you'd stayed to watch." She sheathed the knife. "Odrin's got the last of them at the bone-yard. Sathen's moving the sick through the chapel crypt. We came back for you." She said it flatly, as if it cost her.

"You shouldn't have."

"Tell the tide," Iskra said. "Come on."

The refugees pressed past him, and Voss counted them as they went—an old woman with a birdcage, a man carrying a child on his shoulders, a pair of whalers supporting a third, bandages dark with something not water. He counted fuel loads the way he had been trained, then forced himself to count people instead. The numbers were the same. The meaning was not.

A small shape broke from the line and ran at him; Voss braced for the anger, the slap, the fist.

Pella stopped short, sea-salt hair plastered to her face, standing barefoot in the scum water, looking at his copper hair, his pale eyes, the scar on his chin, the coat that was not a warden's coat.

"You're him," she said. "The burn-man."

It wasn't a question. Voss nodded.

He had seen Pella laugh, mock, teach him the crossing knot with fierce concentration—but never this. It was not forgiveness. It was something blunter. She reached out and took his hand.

"Then you know the way out," she said. "Come on."

She dragged him forward, and the tunnel moved around them.

The vault narrowed beyond a collapsed wall, and they went single file through a gap Voss had widened three nights ago with a borrowed pry-bar. The air thickened with smoke; the crack overhead widened; orange light chased them through the dark. Above, the Spire's foundations roared; the Chantry's guard shouted, organizing against a fire already decided.

The roof of the vault shivered. A slab of brick came down behind them, and the water jumped. Iskra swore and pushed the line forward. Through a shaft of iron bars Voss caught the street: the dry-docks were a wall of white flame, and between the docks and the Spire the granaries burned, sparks riding the wind toward the harbor. The fire was the wall. The fire was the shield. The enforcers would not cross it; there was nothing left to cross on.

"Keep moving," Voss said. "The culvert's safe till the tide."

"How do you know?" the old woman with the birdcage demanded.

"Because I mapped it."

There was no pride in the words. There was no time for pride.

They came to the chapel crypt by a salt-stair, a passage Voss had drawn from a surveyor's line and walked once. Sathen was there with the sick—a tall figure with a soot-thumb birthmark and steady hands—and he looked up as Voss came through the gap and said nothing, and that silence was the kindness it had always been. The crypt stank of wet wool, fever, lamp-oil; the congregation prayed in a murmur barely breath.

A woman coughed—a low, tearing sound—and for a moment the crypt was the Carmine Gate and the cough was the crier's. Voss heard the voice that had once read his edict—cleansed, consented—his own words, young and proud. The crier's young face had looked up at the tower and nodded once, as if to say he had done his part, and Voss had let him finish before pulling the lever. That was the moment he returned to, always: the quarter spread below like a map, the people moving along its streets like ink, and he could have lifted the lever early, could have given the crier a warning to cry instead of an edict, could have shifted the line a hair's breadth to spare the baker's stall. He had done none of it. He had watched. He had wanted to watch.

Pella's hand tightened on his.

"You're shaking," she said.

"I'm remembering," Voss said.

"Is it bad?"

"Yes."

She considered this with the seriousness of a child who had survived worse. "You can remember after," she said. "Right now we're still running."

The tunnel behind the crypt led down, along, up, into a seam Voss had found on the tide-charts: a drain that once carried the bone-yard's leachings to sea. It smelled of salt and old lime. He went first—the man who mapped it should lead through it—and the water rose to his knees, then his waist, and the walls breathed with the turn.

Behind them, the Spire of Charters made a sound like the end of the world, and no one looked back.

They came out into the bone-yard at the seaward end of the Flats, where the tide had pulled the sand from under the breakwater, and the first grey of false dawn lay along the water like a knife laid flat. Odrin's congregation was there—fishers, ferrymen, the one-eyed grandfather from the fishmonger's table—some wading to the waiting boats, Iskra's fleet drawn up in the lee of the breakwater, others watching the sky turn the color of a scab.

The Spire was gone. Where it had stood, a column of ember and smoke turned in the morning wind, and around it the Chantry's dry-docks burned like a second sunrise. The Flats themselves lay black and quiet—empty of people, but unburned. Not one ignition point had fired. The line had been true.

Iskra came up beside him at the water's edge. She did not thank him. She said nothing for a long moment; when she spoke, it was another matter.

"The boats take the women and children first, then the sick, then the rest. You'll be on the last one."

"No," Voss said. "I mapped those tunnels. I'm going back for anyone who didn't make the signal."

It was not courage. It was the same shape as the tower, the aim reversed. He had stood above the fire and watched. He could not undo that. He could only refuse to stand above this one.

Pella had let go of his hand to help an old man to his feet. She came back and stood in front of Voss, squinting up at him in the grey light.

"If you go back," Pella said, "you'll come back."

It was not a question but an order, the way she had ordered him to pay for her day's fish.

"Yes," Voss said.

"Then you owe me another net," she said. "You mended it wrong."

She took his hand again, held it, let it go, and walked toward the boats with her chin up, counting—thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty—

Voss turned back to the tunnel mouth, to the dark, to the city that was hunting him, and went down.

chapters.name: Rain on the Quay
chapters.content:
The tunnel gave him back to the rain. He had gone the length of the black-water channel counting rungs, swept the chapel crypt with his hands because the tallow was gone, climbed the collapsed stair to look out at the Hanging Market's stillness. The Flats had emptied itself true to his lines. Only one thing had been left behind: a doll, snagged on an iron rung where the tide had worked at it, the arm loose at the shoulder, the face cracked, the painted eyes flaking like ash. He worked it free and put it in his coat beside the field-book page.

He came out through the bone-yard leach-drain as false dawn turned gray, and the rain was falling—fine, settling, the kind of rain that washes a city clean whether the city wants it or not. The Spire of Charters stood against the east in a column of ember and smoke, shedding great slow walls of itself into the harbor. The dry-docks burned low and white; the granaries were black ribs; the tithe fleet's lights had gone out. Between the fires lay the Drowned Flats, dark as the inside of a bell, every ignition point cold.

"Late," Iskra said.

She stood at the head of the last boat with rain running off her oilskins. Behind her the congregation moved down the breakwater in a low tide of its own: Odrin steadying an old woman whose hands were shaped by net-mending, Sathen kneeling by a fever cot under a tarpaulin, the one-eyed grandfather holding a birdcage, two whalers supporting a third. Children first, then the sick, then the rest. His plan, carried out without needing his signature.

"We counted forty," she said. "You were not in the count."

"I went back for anyone who missed the signal."

"Find anything?"

He held up the doll.

"Get on the boat."

"Not yet."

"There's nothing left to search. The Flats are empty, the Spire's in the harbor, and the city's hunters are crossing the fire road by evening. You know what you'll be to them now." She said it flat, reading a chart aloud. "The burn-man who turned. They'll hang you in daylight and write that you were always mad."

"I know."

"Then get on the boat. I have a place at the bow—wet this time of year, wind cuts, but it's a place." She paused. This was the part she had to say plainly, and she said it without flinching. "Not a thank you. I don't owe you one, and you don't climb onto my boat forgiven. But the place is yours."

He looked past her at the dying fire against the same sky that had once seen Gullrot burn. The joy in the lever had been real, and it was still real, and he had aimed it at the ledgers and the dry-docks, and the ledgers were ash. It had not made him innocent. Nothing would. The faces in the smoke—the girl at the gate, the baker with his untouched loaf, the crier who had nodded from the wall—would stand with him however far the water carried him.

"I'll take the place," he said. "And I'll leave it when the maps say there's need."

"For what kind of need?"

"Hidden places," he said. "The places where power aims its fire at the innocent and the forgotten. I'll map them. I'll draw the ways out." The design was already forming behind his eyes, all night without ink. The same genius, the same precision. The aim was all.

Rain sang against the stones. The Spire put one last sound into the morning—a long, settling groan, like a whale rolling in its sleep—and the column of smoke went black to gray to white as the harbor closed on it.

Pella came down the breakwater and stopped short of him, bare feet finding the single dry slab. Her sea-salt hair had dried in pale ropes. She looked at him the way she had looked at the fish that morning, deciding what was true.

"Burn-man," she said.

"Yes."

"Did you burn the wrong thing?"

"The right thing."

"Because of the iron? Gref said the iron."

"Because of the iron, and because they called you surgery." He had not said this aloud before. The words came out flat and true as a survey line. "They wrote 'cleansed' and 'consented,' and I wrote it first, for them, fifteen years ago. I know the language. It's for making people into obstructions." He looked at the Flats, black and unburned in the rain. "I aimed at the obstruction instead."

She reached into his coat and took the doll—quick and certain, the way she took anything she meant to keep—and turned the loose arm in her fingers.

"It's broke."

"Yes."

"Will you fix it?"

In the tower at Gullrot he had watched a girl clutch a broken doll and walk back through the quarantine line, and he had not hesitated, and he had never once asked whether the doll could be mended. It had not been on the map. The memory was still there, waiting, the way the faces in the smoke were still there. He knew they always would be.

Pella held out the doll.

He knelt.

The stones were wet; the rain had washed them. He took the doll in both hands—the cracked face, the loose shoulder, the one remaining eye. He had no thread. He had his three effects: the cracked compass, the pencil stub worn to a nub, the map of the Drowned Flats that had become the true map of the people. He drew the pencil stub, found a dry splinter of breakwater wood, and whittled a wedge fine enough to seat in the hollow of the shoulder. He turned the arm, tested the fit, turned it again. When he let go, the joint held. The doll could sit up and wave and not fall apart.

Pella watched him work. She took the doll when he offered it, tested the arm once, and put it inside her coat with the serious care of a woman carrying cargo.

"Will you stay?" she said.

He was still kneeling. The question caught him at the height of the fire—all the years in the Spire, the names in the ledger, the joy in the lever he would never abolish, only aim.

"No," he said. "But I'll stay until every one of you is aboard. And I'll come back when someone needs a map out of the burning."

She nodded as if he had passed a test she had invented on the walk across the stones. Then she turned and went down to the boat, doll under her coat, and began to count the children out of habit—thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty—and the count came out right at the waterline.

Iskra held the stern line, not offering her hand. "Bow seat's wet," she said, and let the line go.

Voss stood. The rain had washed the quay. Behind him the fire was dying against the same sky that had once seen Gullrot burn, and the faces in the smoke had not left, and he knew they never would. But he had knelt in the wet to repair a child's cracked doll, and the joint had held, and the children were on the boats. Whatever came next—the hunters, the hidden places, the long work of mapping where power aimed its flame—he knew what was worth burning for. It had not changed since Gullrot, only aimed. It was the people, not the fuel load.

He waded into the shallows and set his hand on the gunnel where the bow rose with the tide, and did not climb aboard until Pella's voice carried back over the water: "You mended it wrong. You'll owe me another net."

The sun broke through the rain as the fleet pulled for the open channel. Voss stood at the bow, wet and unabsolved, counting the living—and, for the first time since the tower, there was a true line between him and the fire. The same line drawn in flame, and drawn again in rain, and drawn forever in the direction of the children.

errors.pair: The first was a magistrate in grey, her braid coiled like an anchor rope, her fingers stained to the knuckle with ledger-ink.

errors.quote: Fifteen years ago he had walked the ash of Gullrot at dawn and come to the baker's stall at the edge of the fire-line.
errors.pair: His hand reached out and took the bread because it belonged in the hand of a man who had refused it once, twenty-five years ago, and the refusing had not saved anyone.

errors.quote: The Spire of Charters stood against the east in a column of ember and smoke, shedding great slow walls of itself into the harbor.
errors.pair: The Spire was gone. Where it had stood, a column of ember and smoke turned in the morning wind, and around it the Chantry's dry-docks burned like a second sunrise.

errors.quote: The field-book page was still in his coat. Tidal iron. The claims are not.
errors.pair: He took the field-book page from his coat—the page the surveyors had abandoned in Gref's cellar—and handed it to her across the water.
